content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey cordon bleu is a baked or fried roll made from a breast fillet of poultry, stuffed with ham and melted cheese, breaded and cooked until golden. The dish combines the mild flavor of white meat with the savory taste of ham and a stretchy cheese core.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “cordon bleu” comes from French meaning “blue ribbon”, a symbol of culinary excellence.
The original recipe used veal, but modern versions often substitute chicken or turkey for a lighter, more affordable option.
It is commonly served with béchamel, mustard, or creamy sauces.
In the United States, frozen cordon bleu portions are widely available for quick oven preparation.
Variations include adding spinach, mushrooms, or bacon for extra flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Poultry breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and turkey supply niacin (B3) and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Although lower than red meat, poultry still contributes iron needed for blood formation.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (when using chicken breast)
items.content: Chicken breast has less saturated fat than beef, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham and processed cheese are often salty, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats and calories
items.content: Breaded coating and cheese increase calories and saturated fat, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with milk protein allergy or lactose intolerance should use dairy‑free cheese alternatives.

items.title: Risk of undercooked poultry
items.content: Improper cooking may leave the interior insufficiently heated, raising the risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Butterfly the breast, place a slice of ham and a piece of cheese, roll tightly, secure with a toothpick, coat in breadcrumbs and pan‑fry or bake at 180 °C for 25‑30 minutes until golden. Serve hot with mashed potatoes, vegetable ratatouille, or a light salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked cordon bleu can be kept in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 2‑3 days. Frozen portions store up to 3 months when sealed in a vacuum‑packed bag.

classic-mixed-vegetables-canned-reduced-.title: Classic Mixed Vegetables, Canned, Reduced Sodium, Cooked, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Classic mixed vegetables are a blend of carrots, peas, corn and green beans that have been cooked, canned with reduced sodium, and enriched with a small amount of vegetable oil to improve flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vegetables are blanched and sealed shortly after harvest to preserve nutrients.
Reduced sodium is achieved by replacing part of the salt with natural flavor enhancers.
Added vegetable oil helps the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and K.
The mix is commonly used in school cafeterias and quick‑prep meals.
Cans have a long shelf life, typically up to three years.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin B6 and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt levels are beneficial for blood pressure management.

items.title: Added healthy fats
items.content: The vegetable oil contributes omega‑6 fatty acids, important for skin and hair health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene and vitamin C in the mix help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to one or more vegetables in the blend.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Because oil is added, people monitoring fat intake should account for it in their daily totals.

items.title: Pressurized cans
items.content: Damaged or bulging cans can be hazardous and should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The vegetables can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a side dish for meat. They can also be quickly warmed in a pan with a pinch of seasoning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep the contents refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: The Hamburger Wrap Sandwich is a fast‑food item that combines a seasoned meat patty, cheese, vegetables, and sauces wrapped in a soft tortilla. It offers the classic burger flavor with the convenience of a handheld wrap.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger wrap appeared in the United States in the early 2000s as a bun‑less alternative.
Using a tortilla reduces the carbohydrate load compared to a traditional bun.
Variations include chicken, turkey, and vegetarian patties made from beans or soy protein.
A blend of cheeses such as cheddar and mozzarella gives the sandwich a characteristic melt.
Hamburger wraps are often served with fries or onion rings.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sandwich supplies B12 and B6 vitamins important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Vegetables and fiber
items.content: Lettuce, tomato, and onion add dietary fiber and vitamins C and K.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium needed for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The combination of meat, cheese, and sauces can make the wrap calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meat and cheese contain saturated fats that may raise cholesterol if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and cheese often add significant sodium, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; ensure the patty is cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The wrap is designed to be held in one hand; eat it straight from the wrapper or cut it in half. Add extra sauce, fresh veggies, or hot peppers for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared wrap in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze it; reheat in a microwave or skillet before serving.

lamb-or-mutton-rice-and-vegetables-inclu.title: Lamb or Mutton with Rice and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb (or mutton) is sheep meat rich in protein, iron and zinc. Combined with boiled rice and vegetables (carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens) and a tomato‑based sauce, the dish becomes a balanced source of carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb is considered a leaner meat compared with beef, containing less overall fat.
Mutton from a young lamb (lamb) is especially tender and has a milder flavor than meat from an adult sheep.
Rice is a primary source of complex carbohydrates that provide sustained energy.
Broccoli is high in vitamin C and compounds that support the body’s detoxification processes.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale) are rich in vitamin K, essential for blood clotting.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Lamb supplies all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and are vital for hemoglobin formation.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Meat and rice together provide vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant vegetables
items.content: Broccoli and leafy greens are packed with carotenoids and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from carrots and leafy greens promotes healthy bowel movement.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Consuming large portions of fatty lamb cuts may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lamb proteins.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Oxalates in leafy greens
items.content: People prone to kidney stones should moderate intake of spinach and kale.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the lamb into cubes, sear until golden, then simmer with tomato sauce, carrots, broccoli and leafy greens. Cook rice separately until tender and combine with the meat sauce. Serve hot, garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh meat keeps in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days; the prepared dish can be stored in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Freeze individual portions of meat and rice for longer‑term storage, up to several months.

content.title: About
content.content: French fries are deep‑fried strips or wedges made from potato tubers, a staple in school cafeterias and fast‑food outlets. Potatoes provide carbohydrates, vitamin C, potassium and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century.
The first French‑fries recipe appeared in France in the late 19th century.
In Russia, fries are often served with mayonnaise or ketchup.
There are over 4,000 potato varieties, but high‑starch types are preferred for fries.
French fries are a common quick snack in many school canteens.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and protects cells from oxidation.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates in potatoes provide quick energy, important for growing students.

items.title: Beta‑carotene in yellow varieties
items.content: Yellow potatoes contain provitamin A, which the body converts to vitamin A.

items.title: High fat content from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying adds calories and saturated fat, which can affect heart health.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Frequent consumption of heavily salted fries may contribute to high blood pressure.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: French fries are typically served hot, sprinkled with salt, and accompanied by sauces such as ketchup, mayonnaise, or cheese sauce. For a healthier option, bake them in the oven with a small amount of oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fries in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Reheat in an oven or air‑fryer to retain crispness.
